source.title: How does overparametrization affect performance on minority groups?
source.authors: Saptarshi Roy; Subha Maity; Songkai Xue; Mikhail Yurochkin; Yue-Kai Sun

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes how minority-group test risk changes with model overparameterization using random-feature and linear models, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper cites the original double-descent sources and reports its own results on model-size/overparameterization sweeps. The subsampling-versus-ERM comparisons are not rows because they do not measure a sample-size sweep or the double-descent curve. The paper's reported results on the effect of overparameterization are included below.
record.test_reason: Exact asymptotics and simulations of minority- and majority-group test risk as overparameterization γ=N/n grows past interpolation, in random-feature regression, random-feature SVM classification and ridgeless linear regression. This is a new setting (subgroup risk under concept drift) for V4's claim that risk improves past the interpolation point. It is not a reproduction of the deep-network experiments.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that in random-feature regression, overparameterization improves or does not harm minority-group risk of ERM, even in the worst case of identical feature distributions. They also conclude that majority-group subsampling provably improves minority risk and benefits from overparameterization. They note that classification differs (minority error helped at acute and harmed at obtuse angles). They judge ridgeless linear regression inadequate because its risk rises with γ at high SNR.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses high-dimensional asymptotic analysis and simulations of random-feature regression and classification, plus an appendix analysis of ridgeless linear regression; it does not reproduce the original deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The classification result depends on the angle between group coefficients: acute angles favor the minority group, while obtuse angles harm it. In the linear regression appendix, the reported increase in minority error occurs for aligned groups at high signal-to-noise ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: Majority-group subsampling improves minority risk over ERM in the overparameterized regime, most when θ and π are large. It is slightly worse when θ is small (Figures 2 and 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Group-balanced subsampling improves minority-group risk of overparameterized interpolating models.

record.problems: The main findings concern minority-group risk in specified model settings, not the general population risk or the full double-descent curve. Several plotted outcomes have no numerical values in the text. The analysis relies on a stated equal-covariate-distribution assumption for the groups; the text describes classification as a simulation with n = 400 and d = 200.
record.rows_left_out: No additional model-size sweep results relevant to V4 were identified beyond the rows above. The subsampling comparisons in Figure 2 and Figure 5 compare subsampling with ERM rather than reporting the claim's size, epoch, or sample-size curve.

untested.parts: The peak at the interpolation threshold and the underparameterized classical U-curve. The text describes only γ>1 trends, although the figures span γ=0.1 to 10. Overall population risk in the two-group regression setting is also not tested.
Noise or regularization driving the peak, multiple peaks, and behaviour under optimal ridge. Only the ridgeless limit is analysed.

missing.what: Closed-form ridgeless variance limit: τ²γ/(1−γ) for γ<1 and τ²/(γ−1) for γ>1. It diverges at γ=1, a variance-driven peak at the interpolation threshold. Bias s0(1−1/γ) grows for γ>1. This is adapted from Hastie et al.
Figures 1 and 4 plot theoretical and empirical curves across γ from 0.1 to 10, including the underparameterized side and the threshold. The shape there is not recorded in any row.
Ridgeless linear minority MSPE increases with π in both regimes.

record.verdict_notes: Relation is T3 rather than T2: the measure is subgroup risk under concept drift, a new setting for V4, and the study does not test the original question with a different method. Rows r2–r4 are risk components, so the regression verdict rests on r1. No row examines the interpolation peak itself. Neither original source is this paper.

versions.untested_parts: Increasing training sample size near the interpolation threshold.
The full fall-rise-fall curve and its initial descent/peak are not established; results concern minority-group risk in the tested model settings.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across axes.
Whether noise or regularization drives the peak, multiple peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
Whether an effective parameter count converts the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.measure: Limiting minority-group prediction risk (mean squared prediction error).
rows.value: The authors state that risk improves or does not worsen as overparameterization grows; no numeric risk values stated.
rows.locator: Section 3, 'Trend in minority group prediction error for ERM'; Theorem 3.9
rows.note: The result concerns post-threshold minority-group risk in this random-feature regression setting, not the complete double-descent curve.
rows.check: Authors state that both bias and variance decrease or do not increase for γ>1 for any π and θ, so minority risk 'improves or does not harm'. This is the full post-threshold improvement V4 describes, not partial. The baseline is the risk at smaller γ>1, not 'not stated'.

rows.subject: ridgeless least squares estimator
rows.size_stated: Input dimension d; overparameterization ratio γ = d/n
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed minority-group mean squared prediction error as the overparameterization ratio increases.
rows.measure: Minority-group test mean squared prediction error.
rows.value: Figure only; the text states that error increases with growing γ for aligned groups at high signal-to-noise ratio.
rows.note: This is an explicitly described exception in the linear model; numerical plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: At θ=0 the two groups are identical, so this is the overall ridgeless-least-squares risk. Here capacity is tied to input dimension (γ=d/n). The authors attribute the rise to the inductive-bias term at high SNR. The result echoes Hastie et al., which the paper notes.
